items.action: The Tagus has a purely fluvial regime, shaped by rainfall and temperature; climate drove flow variations and thereby the navigability of its waters over time.
items.conditions: flow governed by rainfall and temperature rhythm

items.action: A footnote recalls that prolonged droughts sharply reduced the Tagus flow and made navigation difficult.
items.conditions: estiagens prolongadas (prolonged droughts) reducing the flow

items.action: Upstream of Tancos the Tagus runs in one sinuous channel with high banks; downstream it opens into a wide alluvial plain, over 10 km wide in places.

numbers.what: maximum width of the alluvial plain

items.action: The river's course was not always as seen today; maps show it flowed differently, with lezírias and mouchões (river islands) among the features of the changing landscape.
The Tagus valley was partly silted up within two millennia; as sea level rose and salt water moved upstream, Mesolithic-economy groups occupied the valley.
items.conditions: rising sea level, brackish and salt water reaching upstream

numbers.what: time over which the valley was partly silted up

items.action: Hills running parallel to the river allowed the first inhabitants to settle in defensive hillside villages about 5,000 years ago, facing flat, flooded lands across the river owned by few proprietors.
items.conditions: flat, marshy lands on the opposite bank
items.place: Tagus valley, Vila Franca de Xira
items.who: first inhabitants; the church and the royal house as landowners

items.action: Silting and human occupation gradually reshaped the river and its banks, yet boat traffic kept a vital economic link between Lisbon and Santarém until the 20th century.
items.conditions: silting and human transformation of the banks

items.action: Kings and riverside councils repeatedly disputed the Lezírias of the Tagus, whose configuration kept changing.
In the 19th century, under Queen Maria Pia, the practice of creating accrued lands (Acrescidos) was legislated and banned, though most channels were already silted up.
items.conditions: most channels already filled in, river tending toward a single channel

items.action: At the Cortes of Leiria, Lisbon complained that many estuary inlets in its district were so blocked that wine could barely be loaded, and asked that they be reopened at the expense of the neighbours who shipped wine there.
items.conditions: esteiros blocked
items.place: esteiros of the Termo of Lisboa; Cortes de Leiria
items.who: cidade de Lisboa; vizinhos who embarked wine

items.action: A document records damage from river-course changes near Cardiga: sandy cliffs collapsed onto the Tagus, and flood waters clogged the channel, harming fields, lezírias down to Lisbon, and boat navigation.
items.conditions: collapsing sand banks, silting from floods

numbers.what: length of sand hills along the river

items.action: Strabo described the Tagus as navigable at its mouth by boats of ten thousand amphorae, with flooding turning the plain into a navigable sea and isolating a fertile island.
items.boat: barcos de dez mil ânforas; embarcações de rio
items.conditions: flood season; large boats for much of the route, river craft for the rest

numbers.what: distance of Móron from sea, at most

items.place: Tagus mouth, Móron (identified with Chões de Alpompé, Santarém)

items.action: Fernão Lopes praises the number of ships loading salt and wine at the Sacavém river and at Montijo point opposite Ribatejo under King Fernando.
items.conditions: author notes the number may be exaggerated

numbers.what: ships at each place, per Lopes

items.place: Ribeira de Sacavém; ponta do Montijo

items.action: The Sacavém river space was deep enough for large-draught boats coming from the port of Lisboa to navigate.
items.conditions: sufficient river depth

items.action: River ports followed one another along the right bank toward Santarém, and their prominence continued into later centuries.
items.place: right bank of the Tejo toward Santarém

items.action: River access and navigability shaped daily life in tidal towns such as Alverca, Alhandra, Povos, Vila Nova da Rainha, Azambuja and Porto de Muge.
items.conditions: tidal influence
items.place: Alverca, Alhandra, Povos, Vila Nova da Rainha, Azambuja, Porto de Muge

items.action: Expecting the Castilian king's siege, barcas and batéis brought all available wheat and meat from the Ribatejo lezírias to Lisboa.
items.conditions: siege expected

items.action: After Santarém sided with Castile, people went to the lezírias by boat, bringing back cattle that were salted in vats for provisioning.
items.conditions: Santarém held by Castile

items.action: In 1620 Frei Nicolau de Oliveira counted boats at Tejo ports, showing the importance of river transport at Abrantes, Santarém, Povos and Vila Franca.
The Mestre was advised not to attack the Castilian king at Santarém by barcas, which carry few people and could not go beyond Muge.
items.conditions: very low Tejo water; barcas could not go farther upriver

items.action: Above Azambuja tides weaken; upriver traffic used lateen-sailed, small-tonnage, shallow-draught 'barcos de água acima'.
items.conditions: weak tides

numbers.what: distance of Porto do Sabugueiro upstream of Muge

items.place: above Azambuja; Porto do Sabugueiro, 2 km above Muge

items.action: Crews struggled upriver, fighting winter current and summer sandbanks, pushing boats with poles or towing them from the bank, often running aground.
items.conditions: winter current, summer sand in riverbed

items.action: Under Vila Franca's Manueline foral, barcas docking at the quay with goods had to pay the set charge.
items.cargo: vinegar, flax, roof tiles, firewood, charcoal, fish and shellfish

items.action: At rent-collection time barcas called more intensely at customary places, preferably Porto de Muge, so tenant farmers could meet their obligations.
items.conditions: rent-collection season

items.action: Timber floated down the river to the tercenas (arsenals) in Lisboa, a massive presence on the Lower Tejo.
The forais of Povos and Vila Franca de Xira set payments on outside fish, on a barca of small fish sold, and the tithe owed by fishermen.
King João V authorised the local council to replace a damaged wooden quay, built ten years earlier, with another wooden quay.
items.conditions: damaged wooden quay

numbers.what: years since the old quay was built

items.action: Ferry barges from Almada, Salvaterra, Muge, Constança, Santarém, Arraiolos, Azinhaga and other places also crossed the Tagus.
items.place: Tejo; Almada, Salvaterra de Magos, Muge, Constança (Punhete), Santarém, Arraiolo

items.action: King Afonso V leased the Lisbon toll and fishery, including his right to a tithe on firewood brought through the river mouth and river.
items.conditions: tithe due on firewood

items.action: The charters of Povos and Vila Franca de Xira set a payment on timber coming down the river, suggesting river transport of wood.
items.conditions: logs probably not floated loose, as they could obstruct navigation

items.action: Santarém region supplied Lisbon with cereals, and its royal woodlands were exploited to supply arsenals and construction in Lisbon.
The Tagus served as a busy liquid highway, with goods moving between Lisbon and Santarém in both directions and routes up, down and across.
The Master of Avis sailed 35 barcas and batéis up the Tagus to attack Alenquer, rowing through the night despite a rising tide and unfavourable wind.
items.conditions: tide rising, wind not favourable; stopped about one league from Alenquer

items.action: Two galleys were sent to the residents of Alenquer that year and reached Ponte da Marinha, about a league from the town.
King João II ordered a fleet assembled near Povos and Vila Franca because plague was killing people in Lisbon; it was meant for African campaigns.
items.cargo: 150 horsemen and 1000 foot soldiers, mostly crossbowmen and gunners
items.conditions: plague in Lisbon

items.action: As King Manuel favoured stays at the Almeirim palace, royal and court journeys up the Tagus became frequent, linked to hunting and leisure.
The king travelled by boat from the royal palace at Almeirim to Lisbon (Paço de Xabregas or Paço da Ribeira), using the river as transport.
items.place: Almeirim to Lisbon (Paço de Xabregas, Paço da Ribeira)
items.who: the king (reign of D. Manuel I)

items.action: Royal works in the Tagus valley under D. Manuel I included the imposing quay at Tancos, during a surge in Tagus navigation.
Construction of the Almeirim palace began, adapted from a royal farm's buildings, with land-reclamation (colmatagem) works.
The river served as a natural road for the court, which was drawn to Almeirim by hunting, fertile fields, pleasant climate and views.
Barges carrying Infante D. Henrique's mills were allowed to sail, in any number, from Punhete to Lisbon's river mouth, provided they did not obstruct other barges' navigation.
items.conditions: must not hinder navigation of other barges
items.place: Punhete to the mouth of the Tagus at Lisbon

items.action: Riverside villagers shared the water, managing fresh water through ditches, openings, canals and channels while working the fields along the Tagus.
From the early 16th century barges diversified by function and route; shallow-draught boats without keel or with half keel were built by riverside shipwrights.
items.boat: barca; small-draught boats without keel or half keel
items.conditions: going upriver or on shallow arms required small draught

items.action: The Regimento dos Barqueiros listed the vessel types identifiable on the river.
items.boat: barca, batel, caravelão, muleta (for goods), bateira

items.action: River fishermen lived from the waters, facing strong currents and sometimes tragedy.
items.conditions: currents; seasonal changes

items.action: Shipwrecks were frequent; from the 18th century survivors offered ex-votos at the chapel of Senhor da Boa Morte on the hill above the Tagus.
items.place: chapel of Senhor da Boa Morte above the Tagus

items.action: A document confirming privileges of Vila Franca de Xira fishermen notes they have boats to go fishing and earn their food.
items.who: pescadores de Vila Franca de Xira

items.action: Salted, dried or smoked fish was traded by merchants between the Portuguese coast and the interior of the kingdom.
Fishermen left riverside ports for river fishing, using techniques and net types suited to the size and quality of the fish, refined over many generations.
items.conditions: nets matched to size and quality of fish

items.action: Shad from the Tagus was caught with the boats of Prince Henry and those of Ceuta, and carried to Ceuta to be salted or sold.
items.conditions: fish salted or sold at Ceuta
items.who: fishermen; Prince Henry's and Ceuta's boats

items.action: Santarém traded directly by sea with Flanders and France, and mainly with the Algarve, Seville and Muslim ports of North Africa, since the Tagus was navigable far upstream for merchant ships.
items.conditions: Tagus navigable by merchant ships a long distance

items.action: Smoked or salted fish was exported to Castile, Aragon, Italy, England, Flanders and other regions.
Santarém's representatives at the Évora cortes complained that Castilians and other foreigners came at shad season to buy fish without bringing goods, and asked that buyers carry cargo in exchange.
items.conditions: request that those taking cargo must bring cargo, to keep the land supplied
items.who: procuradores of Santarém; Castilian and foreign buyers

items.action: The 1179 charter for Lisbon regulated the fish trade.
King John I authorised residents of Porto to buy hake and sardines in Lisbon and Setúbal and take them to Porto and elsewhere, without having to give bread in exchange.
items.conditions: no obligation to give bread in return
items.who: residents of Porto; King John I

items.action: The crusader Osberno in 1147 reported so much fish that some believed the Tagus held one part fish to two parts water.

numbers.what: fish share of river volume (as believed)

items.action: Duarte Nunes do Leão (1610) noted shad below Santarém, loaded in large quantity for the kingdom and for parts of Castile.
Meat abstinence days (Wednesdays, Fridays, Advent, Lent) created strong demand for fish; estimates are about 146 days a year, or alternatively 110 to 120 days.
items.conditions: fasting and abstinence rules

numbers.what: days of meat abstinence per year (Coelho)

items.action: Lisbon's toll lease records rents for fisheries of eels, shad and covões on the Tagus.
King Duarte regulates shad fishing on the Tagus, especially around the lezírias and Alqueidão.
Afonso V appoints João do Paço as warden and keeper of the trout of the Muja river.
items.who: D. Afonso V, João do Paço

items.action: Manuel grants the tithe on fish landed at Alhandra and Alverca to D. Martinho de Castelo Branco, as the crown holds it.
items.who: D. Manuel, D. Martinho de Castelo Branco

items.action: Fishermen used many net types along the river: gillnets, drag nets, cast nets and set nets, some mobile and some fixed.
items.gear: redes de emalhar, de arrasto, de lançado e de armar; de armação (fixas)

items.action: Royal measures protect shad: specified net mesh sizes, and live young shad caught in reed traps must be returned to the river.
Use of fine-meshed copéis on bogeiro nets is banned to preserve shad spawn and other fish seed; the ban is proclaimed to fishermen.
items.who: pescadores of Santarém, Abrantes and Punhete

items.action: Fishermen used traps such as ramada, nassa and abarga, and sometimes poisoned water with trovisco, harming fish indiscriminately.
Building any fence or barrier across the Tagus that blocks fish migration is forbidden; offenders forfeit all goods and the barrier is demolished.
items.conditions: penalty: loss of goods, one third to the accuser, two thirds to the crown chamber

numbers.what: share of forfeited goods to accuser

items.action: Beyond professional fishing, people could fish on their own from the riverbank using the available resources.
Angling with rods or lines was done at river beaches, channels, caneiras and fishing spots not owned by lords or the crown.
items.conditions: only where not seigneurial or royal property

items.action: A skilled fisherman might catch fish by hand.
Night fishing is possible on the Tagus as on other medieval rivers, though no specific references exist.
items.conditions: night

items.action: Fisheries in sea and river were a royal right, giving the crown revenues such as tithe and toll, which it could cede to nobles, clergy or councils.
items.conditions: D. Duarte ruled fishery rents and salt pans were royal rights; confirmed by D. Manuel and successors
items.who: the king; D. Duarte; D. Manuel

items.action: Fishers beat the water and threw stones into the river to drive up the catch, a method disliked by those protecting their own fishing grounds.
items.conditions: Conflict with those wanting their fishing spaces unharmed; practice not exclusive to the Mondego

items.action: Fishing on the Tagus followed the daily rhythm of local people, who caught fish either to sell or for their own consumption, with different implications.
Two main markets absorbed the Tagus catch: Santarém, where river fish competed with sea fish, and Lisbon, a larger but more contested market.
items.conditions: In Lisbon, both natives and foreigners bought fish

items.action: Sea fish, some caught at the Tagus mouth, reached Santarém carried upriver by boat, competing with local river fish.
Fishers of Vila Franca de Xira held confirmed privileges to sell their fish, both fresh and salted and cured at home.
items.conditions: Privileges confirmed in 1496
items.who: fishers of Vila Franca de Xira

items.action: All fish and sardines coming through the river mouth owed tithe, even if not sold in Lisbon but taken on to Santarém or elsewhere.
items.conditions: Tithe payable even when not sold in Lisbon

items.action: Some people bought large amounts of fish, loading and shipping it by sea out of the kingdom, and by water from Lisbon to Santarém and elsewhere.
Fish was prepared simply in fishers' homes and sometimes elaborately in wealthy townspeople's homes; at the royal table freshness and quality were ensured, even on meatless days.
Condition of preservation and the means of transport determined whether fish was consumed.
After the bells for terce mass, Lisbon's Ribeira came alive: sea fishers unloaded boats, resellers bought freely, and loading and unloading went on all day.
items.conditions: Began after the bells for the mass of terce
items.who: pescadores de mar; regatões e regateiras

items.action: The Tagus estuary made Lisbon's fortune, with varied products of the kingdom and abroad arriving and leaving, making Lisbon a magnet for the whole realm.
King D. João I's household was supplied with large quantities of fresh and dried fish and shellfish by royal buyer Afonso Anes over twelve years.
items.cargo: dried hake, conger, lamprey, sole, sardines, eels, oysters, lobsters, cuttlefish
items.conditions: Fresh and dried

numbers.what: years of supply by Afonso Anes

items.who: Afonso Anes, comprador régio; D. João I

items.action: Riverside fishers had to obey municipal rules fixing places, hours, sale conditions, prices and quality of fish brought for sale.
items.conditions: Municipal regulations

items.action: Female fish sellers, the regateiras, bought fish to resell and ensure full distribution to consumers.
Tagus waters produced many oysters, and gathering of clams, crabs and shrimp was very fruitful.
Shad teemed in the Tagus; they swam upriver to spawn and the young returned to sea around August/September, giving an abundant catch.
items.conditions: Spawning run upriver; young return to sea in August/September

items.action: King Afonso V, staying at Santarém, had sea fish and shellfish at his table, brought to Santarém by land and river.
Oysters were bought cheaply for the king's table, probably eaten raw though they could be cooked.
A 1482 charter confirmed Catarina Afonso as seller of fish from the crown's tithe on the customs of Santarém.
Fishwives disputed paying tithe on lobsters, claiming they were shellfish and should pay no more than two soldos on a load.

numbers.what: maximum tithe claimed on a load

items.action: Fishwives were forbidden to enter the barcas as muleteers did.
A royal letter of 1462 praised the profitable shad fishery in the Tagus under earlier kings, which supplied the land and drew foreign merchants bringing gold, silver and goods.
items.who: King Afonso V; merchants from Castile

items.action: Fishery owners built tightly woven wicker traps; when young shad descended to sea they added mats and fine doubled nets, killing most fish.
items.conditions: when young shad descend to the sea

items.action: Dead young shad were sold in baskets over the hills like sardines, and large quantities were wasted by being thrown into the water.
Some of the catch reached tables, but fish were also sold for profit at Santarém market or the Ribeira of Lisbon.
King Dinis and his retinue watched the catch of a marvellous sturgeon near Muge; it was recorded for posterity.
Herons, eels, bordalos and mullet were also abundant in the lower medieval Tagus, adding variety to meals.
River floods leaving the bed could halt fishing for long periods and destroy goods, crops, boats and lives.
items.conditions: floods

items.action: Old custom required anyone catching shad and other fish in the Tagus to bring them to the town to be sold there.
items.conditions: fish had to be sold in the town

items.action: A live sturgeon caught at Montalvo near Muge was presented to the king in the Valada fields; it was measured and a notarised document was drawn up.
items.place: Campo de Valada; Montalvo, near Muge
items.who: D. Guedelha, chief rabbi of the Jews; notary Vasco Rodrigues; scribe Lourenço Ma

items.action: A royal letter of sentence mentions fishermen using boats called 'cuus de lobos', catching many fish including eels and bordalos in many ways.
items.cargo: eiroses, eels, bordalos and other fish

items.action: Choice of river fishing boat was governed by the characteristics of the species being caught, whether in rivers, near the coast or at sea.
items.conditions: boat use depended on species caught

items.action: Tagus floods deposited fertile silt on the Valada fields, but long or intense floods rotted crops, delayed germination, broke riverside land and clogged ditches with debris.
items.conditions: flooding

items.action: Islands and channels (lezírias, mouchões) formed and vanished in the riverbed, forcing the water to find new courses and disrupting established navigation routes.
items.conditions: shifting riverbed

items.action: Works from the 16th century and dams in the 20th century ended the struggle between river and people.
Arab writer Ahmede Arrazí described how Tagus floods near Santarém covered flat land, after which late sowings were made and grain ripened with early crops.
items.conditions: flood and recession

items.action: A flood threatened a tenant's contractual obligations on a vineyard at Balea (Valada).
items.conditions: flood

items.action: Farmers dumped detritus into ditches, which slowed water and silted them up, so they had to be reopened at great cost.
Works on the Tagus and its tributary system were promoted during the reign of D. Dinis.
Works changed the Tagus course near Quinta da Cardiga; under D. João V the river was reported shifting near Almeirim.
items.period: 16th century onward; reign of D. João V

items.action: Dams and flood-control works built from the 1950s reduced river load, flood peaks and mean annual flows, and narrowed the Tagus channel, altering its appearance.
items.conditions: flood control

items.action: Records of Tagus floods exist since the 18th century; twentieth-century floods remain vivid in memory.
items.conditions: floods

items.action: During floods fishing work stopped; fish were lost in muddy torrents, making livelihoods harder and raising the threat of hunger for many fishermen.
items.conditions: flood season, muddy water

items.action: Unable to sail during floods, boats were hauled out and kept away from the hostile waters.
items.conditions: flooding

items.action: River people worried most about river ports being ruined by inundation, since future return to the Tagus depended on maintaining them.
items.conditions: flooding

items.action: After waters returned to the bed, fishermen had to wait for muddy banks to recover, then restarted work with occasional freight runs toward Lisbon or supplying local populations.
items.conditions: after floods

items.action: Years of flood and famine were recorded in the Tagus area.
items.conditions: floods and famine

items.action: Farmers and tenants of Alpriate complained to Infante D. Henrique that their silted-up port, where they loaded barcas, needed opening; he agreed and set the cost arrangements for the works.
items.conditions: port silted up; if not openable within a year, open by other means

numbers.what: time to try opening the port

items.who: lavradores e foreiros; Infante D. Henrique

items.action: The king's privilege charter to Vila Franca de Xira fishermen set penalties for misusing fishermen's batéis; half of the fines went to the town's quay works.
items.conditions: penalty for unauthorised use of batéis

numbers.what: share of fines for quay works

items.who: pescadores de Vila Franca de Xira; the king

items.action: Various vessels sailed between Lisbon and Santarém, forming a road of many purposes; both cities shared the medieval Tagus, linked to royal power.
